title: Searching for MobileNetV3
authors: Andrew Howard, Mark Sandler, Grace Chu, Liang-Chieh Chen, Bo Chen, Mingxing Tan, Weijun Wang, Yukun Zhu, Ruoming Pang, Vijay Vasudevan, Quoc V. Le, Hartwig Adam

pages.title: The core idea
pages.subtitle: Co-design the architecture by search, then hand-tune

blocks.html: MobileNetV3 is a family of efficient vision models for phones and other resource-limited hardware. Its central idea is to combine automated architecture search with targeted hand engineering: let an algorithm search for a good backbone, then have humans fix the few parts the search misses.

Two search techniques work together. Platform-aware NAS (neural architecture search) finds the coarse structure of each block, optimizing for accuracy under a latency budget on real hardware. Then NetAdapt tunes the number of filters in each layer one at a time. Finally the authors redesign the most expensive layers by hand and introduce a new activation.

We achieve new state of the art results for mobile classification, detection and segmentation ... MobileNetV3-Large is 3.2% more accurate on ImageNet classification while reducing latency by 20% compared to MobileNetV2.

The result is two models: MobileNetV3-Large (~75.2% top-1 ImageNet, ~20% faster than V2) for higher-resource use and MobileNetV3-Small for very tight budgets. Both push the accuracy-vs-latency frontier outward.

On a phone, what matters is not theoretical FLOPs but actual latency on the device, which depends on memory access patterns, how well operations map to the hardware, and where time is really spent. A layer can be cheap in multiply-adds yet slow in practice, or vice versa.

MobileNetV3 therefore optimizes directly against measured latency, and treats the network design as a search problem rather than a purely manual one. Humans are good at spotting a few structural inefficiencies; search is good at exploring thousands of configurations. The paper uses both, each where it is strongest.

It inherits depthwise-separable convolutions from MobileNetV1 (splitting a normal convolution into a per-channel spatial filter plus a $1\times1$ mixing step) and the inverted-residual, linear-bottleneck block from MobileNetV2, then layers new ideas on top.

The search runs in two phases at two granularities. First, platform-aware NAS searches the global block structure — how blocks are arranged — using a reward that trades off accuracy against on-device latency. This produces a strong starting architecture.

Second, NetAdapt refines it layer by layer. Starting from the NAS model, it repeatedly proposes small reductions to the filter count of individual layers, measures the real latency/accuracy change of each proposal, keeps the best trade-off, and continues until the latency target is met. NAS sets the skeleton; NetAdapt trims the fat.

items: Platform-aware NAS: searches coarse block-level structure under a latency objective.
NetAdapt: fine-tunes per-layer filter counts using measured on-device latency.
The two are complementary — global structure vs. local sizing.

blocks.html: Search tends to leave a couple of layers that are accurate but disproportionately slow — notably the early stem and the final classifier stages. The authors redesign these by hand: they move and shrink the last expensive $1\times1$ expansion (the 'efficient last stage'), cutting latency with no accuracy loss, and reduce the number of filters in the initial layer.

They also add squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules inside the bottleneck blocks. An SE module cheaply learns per-channel importance weights and rescales the channels, giving the network a lightweight form of attention that boosts accuracy for little cost.

The swish activation, $x \cdot \sigma(x)$, improves accuracy but its sigmoid is expensive to compute on mobile hardware (and awkward to quantize). MobileNetV3 replaces it with a piecewise-linear approximation called hard-swish (h-swish):

Reading this: $\text{ReLU6}(z) = \min(\max(z, 0), 6)$ is a clipped ReLU that hardware already supports efficiently. The fraction is a cheap, piecewise-linear stand-in for the sigmoid, so h-swish behaves like swish but uses only fast, quantization-friendly operations. The authors apply it mainly in the deeper half of the network, where it helps most and the feature maps are smaller (so the cost is low).

On ImageNet, MobileNetV3-Large reaches about 75.2% top-1 accuracy while being roughly 20% faster than MobileNetV2 at comparable accuracy — a clear improvement on the speed-accuracy trade-off. MobileNetV3-Small targets the very-low-latency regime and beats prior small models at similar speed.
Ablations confirm every ingredient pulls its weight: the searched structure, the redesigned expensive layers, the SE modules, and h-swish each contribute measurable accuracy or latency gains.

The backbone transfers to other tasks. As a detection feature extractor it improves the speed-accuracy trade-off on COCO over MobileNetV2. For semantic segmentation the paper introduces Lite Reduced ASPP (LR-ASPP), an efficient segmentation head that pairs with the V3 backbone to deliver strong Cityscapes accuracy at low latency.
MobileNetV3-Large LR-ASPP is 34% faster than MobileNetV2 R-ASPP at similar accuracy for Cityscapes segmentation.

MobileNetV3 showed that the best efficient models come from combining automated search with human insight, and from optimizing against measured hardware latency rather than proxy FLOPs. Its components — h-swish, SE in mobile blocks, the efficient last stage — became common ingredients in later efficient architectures.

items: Combined platform-aware NAS (global structure) with NetAdapt (per-layer sizing).
Hand-redesigned the expensive stem/last stage and added squeeze-and-excitation blocks.
Introduced h-swish, a quantization-friendly, hardware-efficient activation.
MobileNetV3-Large: ~75.2% ImageNet top-1, ~20% faster than V2; strong detection and segmentation transfer.
